```{r si-setup, include=FALSE}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(here); library(dplyr); library(ggplot2); library(patchwork)
})
source(here("paper", "_helpers.R"))
ladder <- readRDS(here("paper", "cache", "fig2_glmer_ladder.rds"))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%", dpi = 300
)
```

```{r fig-cross-sectional-confound, fig.width=9, fig.height=4}
#| label: fig-cross-sectional-confound
#| fig-cap: "Non-identifiability of growth models in cross-sectional data. Panels show the same simulated data, reflecting the possibility of stable between-child intercept differences (A) vs. varying growth slopes (B)."
# Why longitudinal data are needed to identify per-child acceleration.
#
# A single cross-sectional snapshot — one ability estimate per child at
# their observed age — is consistent with qualitatively different
# individual-trajectory structures. We draw ONE set of cross-sectional
# points (identical in both panels) and overlay two generative stories
# that each pass through every point exactly:
#   (A) stable between-child differences: every child shares the
#       population slope and differs only in intercept (parallel lines);
#   (B) diverging trajectories: every child starts from a common early
#       ability and differs in slope (a fan).
# With one observation per child the two are indistinguishable — only
# repeated measurement of the same child reveals which holds.

set.seed(42)
N         <- 28
a0        <- 6                       # reference age; log(t/a0) > 0 over 8-30
kappa_pop <- 2.5                     # population acceleration (slope on log-age)
sigma_xi  <- 1.0                     # between-child intercept spread

ages_obs <- runif(N, 8, 30)
L_obs    <- log(ages_obs / a0)
# cross-sectional cloud: ability rises with log-age + between-child noise
theta_obs <- kappa_pop * L_obs + rnorm(N, 0, sigma_xi)
pts <- data.frame(age = ages_obs, theta = theta_obs)

age_grid <- seq(8, 30, length.out = 60)
L_grid   <- log(age_grid / a0)

# (A) parallel: each child same slope kappa_pop, intercept set to hit point
parallel <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(N), function(i) {
  xi <- theta_obs[i] - kappa_pop * L_obs[i]
  data.frame(child = i, age = age_grid, theta = xi + kappa_pop * L_grid)
}))

# (B) fanning: common early origin theta0, slope set to hit point
theta0 <- min(theta_obs) - 1.5       # origin below the cloud so all slopes > 0
fanning <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(N), function(i) {
  kappa_i <- (theta_obs[i] - theta0) / L_obs[i]
  data.frame(child = i, age = age_grid, theta = theta0 + kappa_i * L_grid)
}))

yr <- range(theta_obs) + c(-1, 1)
mk <- function(traj, ttl) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_line(data = traj, aes(age, theta, group = child),
              color = "#2b8cbe", alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_line(data = data.frame(age = age_grid,
                                theta = kappa_pop * L_grid +
                                        (mean(theta_obs) - kappa_pop * mean(L_obs))),
              aes(age, theta), linetype = "dashed",
              color = "grey45", linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_point(data = pts, aes(age, theta), size = 1.3, color = "grey15") +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = yr) +
    labs(x = "age (months)", y = expression(ability~theta), title = ttl) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}

mk(parallel, "(A) stable between-child differences (intercepts vary)") +
mk(fanning,  "(B) diverging trajectories (slopes vary)")
```

```{r fig-glmer-ladder-linear, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
#| label: fig-glmer-ladder-linear
#| fig-cap: "Linear ability growth model variants. See main text for model fit comparisons."
# Supplemental Figure 2: the LINEAR-age model variants (A, B, C, D),
# matching the main-text Figure of the log-age models. Same data and
# plotting conventions; here ability grows linearly in age rather than
# in log-age. Within the observed age range the fits are very similar
# to the log-age models (see main text dAIC comparison).
qtiles <- ladder$qtiles |>
  filter(model %in% c("A", "B_lin", "C_lin", "D_lin")) |>
  mutate(qprob_f = factor(qprob, levels = c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9),
                          labels = c("0.1", "0.25", "0.5", "0.75", "0.9")))
emp <- ladder$emp |>
  mutate(child_lang = paste(lang_slug, child_id, sep = "::"))

model_lab <- c("A"     = "(A) accumulator",
               "B_lin" = "(B) + pop. acceleration",
               "C_lin" = "(C) + per-child efficiency",
               "D_lin" = "(D) + per-child acceleration")
qtiles$model_label <- factor(model_lab[qtiles$model], levels = model_lab)
lang_lab <- ladder$lang_labels
emp$lang_label    <- factor(lang_lab[emp$lang_slug],    levels = lang_lab)
qtiles$lang_label <- factor(lang_lab[qtiles$lang_slug], levels = lang_lab)
emp_facet <- bind_rows(lapply(names(model_lab), function(m)
  emp |> mutate(model_label = factor(model_lab[m], levels = model_lab))))

qt_fan    <- filter(qtiles, model %in% c("C_lin", "D_lin"))
qt_median <- filter(qtiles, !model %in% c("C_lin", "D_lin"),
                    qprob_f == "0.5")

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = filter(emp_facet,
                          language %in% c("English (American)", "Norwegian")),
            aes(age, vocab, group = child_lang),
            color = "grey25", alpha = 0.03, linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_line(data = filter(emp_facet,
                          !(language %in% c("English (American)", "Norwegian"))),
            aes(age, vocab, group = child_lang),
            color = "grey25", alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_line(data = qt_fan,
            aes(age, vocab, color = qprob_f, group = qprob_f,
                linewidth = ifelse(as.character(qprob_f) == "0.5", 0.95, 0.55))) +
  geom_line(data = qt_median,
            aes(age, vocab, color = qprob_f, group = qprob_f),
            linewidth = 0.95) +
  facet_grid(lang_label ~ model_label, scales = "free_y", space = "fixed",
             switch = "y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = WORDBANK_PALETTE, name = "Percentile",
                     labels = c("10th", "25th", "50th", "75th", "90th"),
                     drop = FALSE) +
  scale_linewidth_identity() +
  labs(x = "Age (months)", y = "Productive vocabulary") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 8, face = "bold"),
        strip.placement = "outside",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom",
        panel.spacing = unit(0.4, "lines"))
```

```md
## Relation to prior accumulator models  [draft for promotion — MCF to review]

Our model is one member of a family of accumulator models of early
vocabulary, and the family is easiest to compare in a single set of
coordinates. Writing the latent ability of child $i$ on word $j$ at
age $t$ as

$$\eta_{ij}(t) = \log r_i + \log \alpha_i + \kappa_i \log t - \delta_j,$$

every prior model in this tradition is a special case that fixes one or
more of three quantities: the between-child variance in efficiency
($\sigma_\alpha$), the population scaling exponent ($\kappa_{\text{pop}}$),
and — critically — the between-child variance in that exponent
($\sigma_\kappa$). Mapping each prior model into these coordinates makes
the comparison structural rather than notational.

**McMurray [-@mcmurray2007]** is a pure accumulator: every word fills at a
single unit rate ($\kappa = 1$) and children do not differ
($\sigma_\alpha = \sigma_\kappa = 0$). Its central insight is that the
*vocabulary* curve accelerates even when the underlying rate does not,
because ability sweeps through a distribution of word difficulties — the
construction reproduced in panel (A) of our schematic. Acceleration here
is a population-level property of the difficulty distribution, not a
change in the child. This corresponds to our M1.

**Mitchell & McMurray [-@mitchell2009]** add a leverage term: already-known
words speed the acquisition of new ones. They prove that this feedback
shifts *when* words are acquired but cannot manufacture acceleration that
is not already present in the difficulty distribution. In our coordinates
it moves the timing of acquisition without changing $\kappa$, and — being
non-linear in accumulated vocabulary — it is the one prior model that does
not embed cleanly in the linear predictor above.

**Hidaka [-@hidaka2013]** introduces a rate-change process in which ability
grows as $t^{D+1}$; his exponent $D$ is exactly $\kappa_{\text{pop}} - 1$
in our notation, so $D > 0$ is population-level acceleration
($\kappa_{\text{pop}} > 1$). This is our M2. The acceleration is shared
across children ($\sigma_\kappa = 0$). Hidaka relates $D$ to word
imageability — i.e. a *per-word* scaling exponent — which is an
interesting direction we do not pursue here.

**Mollica & Piantadosi [-@mollica2017]** model each word as a Gamma
waiting-time process in which acquisition occurs after roughly ten
"effective learning instances." In our coordinates this is again a pure
accumulator ($\kappa = 1$); the per-word variation they capture lives in
the Gamma shape parameter, which corresponds to a per-word discrimination
(a 2PL extension) rather than to per-child structure.

**Kachergis et al. [-@kachergis2022]** are the first to free
$\sigma_\alpha$: they cast vocabulary as a Rasch model in which each child
has their own latent ability, unifying the accumulator and item-response
traditions. This is our M3. But the scaling exponent remains shared across
children ($\sigma_\kappa = 0$), and the model is proposed as a framework
rather than fit to longitudinal individual data.

Reading down this list, the literature progressively frees parameters —
McMurray fixes all three, Hidaka frees $\kappa_{\text{pop}}$, Kachergis
frees $\sigma_\alpha$ — but every model holds $\sigma_\kappa = 0$.

| Model | $\sigma_\alpha$ | $\kappa_{\text{pop}}$ | $\sigma_\kappa$ | per-word $\delta_j$ |
|---|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| McMurray (2007)            | 0 | 1     | 0 | free |
| Mitchell & McMurray (2009) | 0 | 1     | 0 | free + leverage |
| Hidaka (2013), rate-change | 0 | $D+1$ | 0 | free |
| Mollica & Piantadosi (2017)| 0 | 1     | 0 | free |
| Kachergis et al. (2022)    | free | free | 0 | free |
| **This work (M4)**         | **free** | **free** | **free** | **free** |

Our contribution is to free $\sigma_\kappa$: children differ not only in
how efficient they are but in how steeply their learning accelerates. This
is the load-bearing addition — it is what lets the model fit the widening
fan of trajectories with age (M4 vs M3 in the main text). It is also a
falsifiable claim rather than a parameter convenience: if $\sigma_\kappa$
were near zero the model would collapse onto Kachergis et al., but the
estimated per-child slope variance is well above zero and large relative
to the efficiency variance $\sigma_\alpha$ (main text, Figure 2 and
Results).
```

```md
## Comparing children and language models on one slope axis  [draft for promotion — MCF to review]

The comparison to language models in Figure 6 places children and models
on a single, literally shared axis: the slope of the acquisition sigmoid
in log-experience. Both populations have sigmoidal per-word acquisition
curves, and the slope of that sigmoid is directly comparable.

On the child side, our linear predictor makes this slope exact.
Differentiating $\eta_{ij}(t)$ with respect to $\log t$ gives $\kappa_i$:
the logit-probability that a child produces a word rises linearly in
log-age with slope equal to that child's scaling exponent. The per-child
sigmoid slope *is* $\kappa_i$, by construction.

On the model side, @chang2022 fit a four-parameter logistic to each
(model, word) pair, describing how the model's surprisal for a word falls
over training. Re-expressed as the fraction of a word's surprisal
reduction achieved so far, their fit is a sigmoid in
$\log_{10}(\text{training steps})$ with slope $1/\text{scale}_w$.
Dividing by $\ln 10$ converts this to natural-log units — the same units
as $\kappa_i$ — so the two slopes can be read off the same axis.

The result is a striking separation (Figure 6). Language models cluster
near a slope of one — the unit-accumulator boundary, where each log-unit
of additional experience yields a fixed increment of learning. Children
sit in a broad distribution roughly an order of magnitude higher. On the
shared axis, children's word learning accelerates with experience in a way
that these models' does not.

Three caveats bound this comparison. First, the variability is asymmetric:
children's slopes vary across *children*, whereas a single model is a
deterministic learner, so model slopes vary across *words* within a run
rather than across replicate learners. Second, the steep child slope is
the *per-child* quantity; a researcher fitting a single sigmoid to
cross-sectional Wordbank data per word would recover a shallower slope,
because marginalizing over the population attenuates it. Third, the models
in @chang2022 were trained on adult written text rather than
child-directed speech, so part of the gap could reflect the input
distribution rather than the learner. Models trained directly on CHILDES
(Feng et al., forthcoming) provide the matched-input test: if the gap
largely persists, it is structural; if it shrinks substantially, the input
distribution is doing more of the work than we currently attribute to it.
```

```md
## Connection to neural scaling laws  [draft for promotion — MCF to review; most speculative of the three]

The per-word picture above connects to a more familiar aggregate
phenomenon: neural scaling laws. A model's loss falls as a smooth power
law in the amount of training data, and this descent is remarkably
regular — different runs, and different model sizes, trace nearly the same
curve (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). Our per-word analysis
is the micro-level counterpart of that regularity. Each word is acquired
along a sigmoid whose slope sits near the unit-accumulator value, and the
spread of those slopes — across words and across runs — is small. The
aggregate smoothness of scaling laws and the per-word $\kappa \approx 1$
we recover are two views of the same property: language models convert
experience into knowledge as near-pure accumulators, with little
instance-to-instance variation.

Children depart from this picture on both axes at once. Their per-instance
scaling is far steeper ($\kappa \approx 10$), and they vary substantially
from one another in that exponent ($\sigma_\kappa$ well above zero). The
"data gap" between children and language models [@frank2023; @warstadt2023]
is therefore not only that children reach adult competence from orders of
magnitude less input. It is that children convert experience into knowledge
through a different scaling relationship — steeper, and far more variable
across individuals — than the one that scaling laws describe for models.

This connection is analogical rather than formal: scaling laws characterize
aggregate loss, whereas our $\kappa$ characterizes per-item acquisition,
and the two need not move together. We offer it as a framing for why the
data gap may be harder to close than raw data counts suggest.
```
